name: Crown of Aragon
summary: The Crown of Aragon was a composite monarchy. Its kingdoms and principalities shared sovereign and dynastic politics, but retained different institutions, laws, and forms of representation.
notes: Dynastic union of entities with their own laws and institutions; the components show their joint history, not simultaneous possession in 1137. Each government and polygon is dated separately.

uniones.titulo: Castile and Aragon: a composite monarchy
uniones.resumen: Isabel and Fernando linked their crowns through marriage and shared government. Their heirs accumulated rights of different origins.
uniones.instituciones: The crowns retained their own institutions, taxation and laws. Isabel's death in 1504 separated her successive trajectories before Charles's accession; the decrees of Nueva Planta later transformed that organization.

personas.nombre: Eleanor of Aragon, Queen of Cyprus
personas.resumen: Wife of Peter I and mother of Peter II, she played a prominent political role after her husband's murder. She was involved in court battles and in her relations with Genoa. She ended up returning to the domains of the Crown of Aragon.
King of Naples, 1414–1435. King of the Anjou-Durazzo dynasty.

eventos.titulo: Marriage of Isabella of Castile and Fernando of Aragon
eventos.descripcion: The marriage union binds the two main crowns of the Iberian Peninsula without merging them legally into a single kingdom.
The capitulation of Granada to Elizabeth I and Ferdinand II put an end to the Nasser Emirate; Muhammad XII, Boabdil, surrendered the city.
Charles V demands that Luther withdraw. The refusal of the reformer and the political protection of Frederick the Wise transformed a theological dispute into a constitutional problem of the Empire.
Imperial forces defeat the French army and capture King Francis I.
Mutinous imperial troops plunder Rome during the Italian Wars.
The agreement legally accepts the coexistence of Catholic and Lutheran territories within the Empire and recognizes that religious unity can no longer be restored by simple imperial imposition.
Charles V progressively divided his dominions between the Spanish branch and the Austrian branch of the Habsburgs.

The Holy League fleet, led by Don John of Austria and composed mainly of forces of the Spanish Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States, defeated the Ottoman navy of Ali Baja after hours of galley-to-galley combat. The Ottoman center collapses, Uluç Ali manages to save part of his wing and thousands of fighters are killed, wounded or captured. The victory did not drive the Ottoman Empire out of the Mediterranean, but destroyed much of its combat fleet and became a huge political and symbolic victory for the coalition.
Philip II's naval expedition against England failed after fighting, logistical problems and adverse weather.

eventos.titulo: Alberico da Barbiano and the Company of San Jorge
eventos.descripcion: Alberico da Barbiano symbolizes the consolidation of arms companies led by Italian captains, capable of competing with large foreign companies.

eventos.titulo: The fall of Braccio da Montone
eventos.descripcion: The Battle of L'Aquila destroys the power of Braccio da Montone and accelerates the rise of a new generation of captains, including Francesco Sforza and Niccolò Piccinino.

eventos.titulo: Charles V is elected King of the Romans
eventos.descripcion: The succession of Maximilian I makes the imperial election a European competition. Charles brings together the imperial crown with a dynastic heritage that stretches from the Netherlands to Spain and America.
In the absence of a male heir, Charles VI attempts to secure the indivisibility of the Habsburg dominions and the succession of his future daughter Maria Teresa.
Philip Melanchthon presents before Charles V a systematic exhibition of the Lutheran faith, supported by several princes and cities of the Empire.
Charles V defeated the League of Esmalkalde and captured its two great leaders, but the military victory failed to restore the religious unity of the Empire.
Rodrigo Borja ascends to the pontificate as Alexander VI and the career of his sons makes the Borgia family an Italian political power.
The death of Francis of Anjou makes Henry of Navarre a presumed heir. Henry of Guisa reorganizes the Catholic League, backed by Spain, to prevent a Protestant from inheriting the French crown.

eventos.titulo: Benefit: The Anjou take the kingdom
eventos.descripcion: Charles of Anjou, supported by the papacy, defeats and kills Manfredo at Benevento. The Hohenstaufen monarchy loses effective control of Sicily and Naples.

eventos.titulo: Conradino: the last attempt by Hohenstaufen
eventos.descripcion: Conradino invades Italy to recover his family's inheritance, but is defeated at Tagliacozzo and executed in Naples. Charles of Anjou remains as owner of the former kingdom of Hohenstaufen.
After years of war, the Sicilians support Frederick, son of Peter III and Constance of Hohenstaufen. The island develops its own political line in front of the Angevine Naples.

The peace of Caltabellotta recognizes Frederick on the island and the Anjou on the mainland. The old Sicilian monarchy is politically divided between Trinacria and the kingdom that historiography will call Naples.

Alfonso V of Aragon defeated the Angevine resistance and entered Naples. For the first time since the Vespera, a single monarch controls Aragon, Trinacria and the continental kingdom, although the crowns retain separate identities.

eventos.titulo: Alfonso's legacy is split up again.
eventos.descripcion: At the death of Alfonso V, Aragon and Trinacria passed to his brother John II, while Naples remained for his son Ferdinand. Personal union does not become a stable merger of crowns.
Louis XII and Ferdinand the Catholic agree to divide the kingdom of Frederick I. Cooperation is short-lived: disputes over the boundaries of partition turn former allies into enemies.

eventos.titulo: Cerignola: The Great Captain Changes the War
eventos.descripcion: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba's forces defeated the French at Cerignola. The combined use of infantry, field fortifications and firearms consolidated Aragonese position in southern Italy.
A second major victory for the Grand Captain forces the French forces to retreat. The balance born of the 1500 cast is definitely broken in Fernando's favor.

eventos.titulo: Fernando brings together Naples and Trinacria under his crown
eventos.descripcion: The French defeat leaves Ferdinand the Catholic as king of Naples besides Trinacria. The two parts of the former Sicilian monarchy once again share sovereignty, although they will continue to be administered as separate kingdoms.

eventos.titulo: Pius V gets the Holy League
eventos.descripcion: Pius V achieves an agreement between the Spanish Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States. Philip II contributes an essential part of the resources and his half-brother Don John of Austria receives the supreme command of the Allied fleet.

In Messina a heterogeneous army of Spanish, Venetians, pontiffs, Genoese and other Italian contingents is concentrated. Coordinating different interests is almost as important as bringing ships together.

The League has Barbarigo in the left wing, Don Juan and Colonna in the centre, Gianandrea Doria in the right and Álvaro de Bazán in the front of the reserve. In front of them, Ali Baja leads the Ottoman center and Uluç Ali leads the wing facing Doria.

In the center, the Royal gallery of don Juan and the Sultanate of Ali Bajá are stuck in a struggle of successive approaches, archbuildings and reinforcements. The fall of Ali Baja and the capture of his ship disorganize the Ottoman center and turn the central battle into the symbolic core of victory.

Barbarigo is fatally wounded in the Christian left wing. On the opposite end, Uluç Ali takes advantage of the open space during the Doria maneuver and hits several league galleys. The reserve of Álvaro de Bazán goes to close the gap, while Uluç Ali manages to retreat with part of his ships.

eventos.titulo: The King's resignation does not force the island
eventos.descripcion: Jaime II agreed to abandon his Sicilian claim to Anagni, but the Sicilians refused to return to the Angevine dominion. They elected their brother Federico and forced the House of Barcelona to split over the future of the island.

Caltabellotta had foreseen Federico's life-long rule and a later solution favorable to the Anjou. By associating Peter to the throne, the island house defended its own hereditary transmission. The peace of 1302 had not closed the dispute.

eventos.titulo: The death of the heir leaves the crown to a granddaughter
eventos.descripcion: Charles, Duke of Calabria died before Robert. Juana inherited the crown and had to assert her authority before branches of her own family. The murder of Andrés d'Anjou later triggered the invasions of Louis of Hungary.

eventos.titulo: Another peace redefines the two Sicilies
eventos.descripcion: The papal mediation gave a new framework to the recognition of Frederick as king of Trinacria, with obligations towards Juana. The names of Sicily and Trinacria expressed disputed rights in addition to a geographical separation.

eventos.titulo: Two branches argue over an inheritance
eventos.descripcion: Juana had chosen Louis of Anjou as heir, but Charles of Durazzo conquered the kingdom. His death and Juana's left the next generation with a war between Anjou and Durazzo, not a peaceful succession.

Maria and Martin arrived in Sicily with Aragonese support to impose themselves on the barons. The queen's hereditary legitimacy was not enough without military ability. The island's government was once again closely linked to the Crown of Aragon.

eventos.titulo: A Vasa is elected King of Poland
eventos.descripcion: Sigismund III Vasa arrives at the Polish-Lithuanian Crown as grandson of Sigismund I and Swedish prince. The election opens a stage in which the Commonwealth directly crosses with the Baltic dynastic struggles.

eventos.titulo: Alexander III of Scotland is dead
eventos.descripcion: Alexander III's accidental death leaves his granddaughter Margaret of Norway as heiress and opens a decisive succession crisis for Scotland.

eventos.titulo: Magnus brings Sweden and Norway together
eventos.descripcion: The Norwegian inheritance by Ingeborg and the Swedish election converge on Magnus Eriksson, still a child. Each kingdom keeps its own counsel and laws.
Margaret's son, now king of Denmark, inherits the Norwegian crown from Haakon VI. The minority government is in Margarita's hands.
Erik's coronation expresses the project of a common monarch for Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Margaret maintains a decisive authority and kingdoms retain their own institutions.
The Swedish revolt led by Engelbrekt Engelbrektsson opens a phase of regency, restoration and deposition. The government of the union ceases to be continuous.
Sten Sture the Elder's victory over Christian I strengthens Swedish political autonomy in the context of the union crisis.

After the death of Sten Sture the Younger, Christina Gyllenstierna supports the resistance of Stockholm. The capitulation, the coronation of Christian II and the executions precipitate a new rebellion.
Gustav's election consolidated the Swedish break with Kalmar. Denmark and Norway remain linked, now under Frederick I after the deposition of Christian II.
The Kiel deal was followed by a Norwegian constitutional process and a war with Sweden. The new union maintains the Norwegian constitution with amendments.

people.ISABAUST: Daughter of Philip the Beautiful and Joanna of Castile, she married Christian II of Denmark. Her marriage connected the Kalmar crisis to the Habsburg network. After Cristian's deposition she accompanied the family to exile in the Netherlands, where she died.
people.CRISTIAN2DIN: He tried to strengthen the royal power in the Scandinavian kingdoms. The Stockholm bloodbath intensified Swedish resistance and contributed to the break-up of the union.
people.INGEBORGDIN: Consort of the Estridsen dynasty. Her life was connected with France, Denmark.
people.ANADINAMARCA: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with England, Scotland, Denmark.
people.CATALINAJAG: Daughter of Sigismund I of Poland and Bona Sforza, she married John of Sweden, future John III. Her son Sigismund brought together the Polish election and the Swedish heritage. The Jagellón-Vasa connection explains that accumulation, but political and religious differences eventually separated the crowns.
people.JUAN3SUECIA: He deposed his brother Henry XIV and sought an intermediate religious policy. His marriage to Catherine Jagiellon linked the Vasa to the Polish succession.
people.SEGIS3VASA: King of Poland and for a time also of Sweden. His dual heritage of Vasa and Jagellón fueled long wars over the Baltic and dynastic conflicts between the two crowns.
people.ANNADENMARKSAX: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Saxony.
people.ANNASOPHIEDENSAX: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Saxony.
people.SVERKER2SUE: King of Sweden since 1196. He was deposed by Erik Knutsson in 1208 and died in 1210 trying to regain the throne.
people.INGEGERDBIRGERSUE: Consort of the Bjälbo dynasty. Their life was connected with Sweden.
people.ERIK10SUE: King of Sweden since 1208 after defeating Sverker II. He was the first Swedish king to be crowned.
people.RICHEZADIN: Consort of the Estridsen dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark, Sweden.
people.JUAN1SUE: King of Sweden, 1216–1222. King of the Sverker dynasty.
people.ERIK11SUE: King of Sweden since 1222, deposed between 1229 and 1234. His reign was dominated by great nobles, including Birger Jarl, father of his successor.
people.KNUT2SUE: Canuto the High, king of Sweden since 1229 after deposing Erik XI. He died in 1234 and Erik regained the throne.
people.INGEBORGERIKSUE: Noble of the Erik dynasty. Her life was connected with Sweden.
people.BIRGERJARL: A Swedish magnate and regent associated with the consolidation of the monarchy and the expansion of royal power. The dynasty of his descendants would rule Sweden for generations.
people.VALDEMARSUE: Son of Birger Jarl, elected king of Sweden in 1250 under his father's regency. His brother Magnus deposed him in 1275.
people.MAGNUS3SUE: Magnus Ladulås, king of Sweden since 1275 after deposing his brother Valdemar. He strengthened the royal authority and granted tax privileges to the nobility who served on horseback.
people.HELVIGHOLSTEIN: Consort of the Schaumburg dynasty. Her life was connected with Holstein, Sweden.
people.BIRGERSUE: King of Sweden since 1290. He imprisoned his brothers Erik and Valdemar at the Nyköping banquet (1317), where they died; the nobility's reaction drove him out of the kingdom.
people.ERICMAGNUSSONSUE: Son of Magnus III and brother of King Birger. His rivalry with Birger was part of a family crisis that ended his captivity and death. His marriage to Ingeborg of Norway was decisive: his son Magnus reunited the Norwegian heritage and the Swedish election in 1319.
people.INGEBORGNORUEGA: Daughter of Haakon V and Euphemia. Her marriage to Erik Magnusson linked Norway to the Swedish house of Bjälbo. Her son Magnus inherited Norway and was elected king of Sweden in 1319. Ingeborg intervened in minority politics, although the councils of both kingdoms later limited her authority.
people.MAGNUS4SUE: He reunited Sweden and Norway as a child through two distinct paths: Swedish choice and inheritance from his maternal grandfather Haakon V. His reign saw expansion into Scania and serious internal conflicts.
people.BLANCANAMUR: Daughter of the Count's House of Namur and wife of Magnus Eriksson. Her sons Erik and Haakon participated in the power divisions of Sweden and Norway.
people.ERIK12SUE: King of Sweden, 1356–1359 (corregent). King of the Bjälbo dynasty.
people.HAAKON6NOR: Son of Magnus Eriksson and Blanche of Namur. He ruled Norway and briefly shared Swedish royalty with his father. He married Margaret, daughter of Valdemar IV of Denmark. His son Olaf inherited Norway when he was already Danish king: the marriage prepared a union whose access occurred on different dates.
people.EUPHEMIASUE: Sister of Magnus Eriksson and daughter of Ingeborg of Norway. She married Albert II of Mecklenburg. Her son Albert was king of Sweden, while the descendants of her son Henry led up to Eric of Pomerania. It is a key link between Bjälbo, Mecklemburg and the Kalmar Union.
people.ALBERTOSUE: Albert of Mecklemburg, King of Sweden from 1364 with the support of the Swedish nobility. His conflict with Margaret I ended with her defeat at Åsle (1389).
people.VALDEMAR4DIN: He restored much of the territorial power of the Danish monarchy after a period of fragmentation and striving. His daughters Ingeborg and Margarita created two paths of dynastic continuity. Margaret's son, Olaf, was elected king; Ingeborg's descendants later brought Eric of Pomerania.
people.HEDVIGSCHLESWIG: Consort of the Estridsen dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark, Schleswig.
people.MARGARITA1NORD: Queen and regent who brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden together under her authority and laid the foundations of the Kalmar Union. She was the dominant political figure in northern Europe at the end of the 14th century.
people.ERICOPOMERANIA: A nephew of Margaret, he was promoted to heir and recognized in the three kingdoms before the coronation of Kalmar in 1397. Margaret continued to lead politics until 1412.
people.CRISTOBALBAVSUE: Nephew of Eric of Pomerania by his mother Catherine. He was elected separately in Denmark, Sweden and Norway after his uncle's deposition. He married Dorothea of Brandenburg and died childless. The new crisis allowed the crowns to initially take different paths.
people.CARLOS8SUE: Charles Knutsson, of the House of Bonde, alternated stages as king of Sweden with exile and restorations. He also claimed and briefly exercised the Norwegian royalty against Christian I.
people.CRISTIAN1NORD: Count of Oldburgh elected King of Denmark in 1448. It later reunited Norway and, for a shorter period, Sweden.
people.ESTENSTUREVIEJO: Regent of Sweden for two periods, he held wide autonomy from the kings of the union. His victory at Brunkeberg in 1471 cemented that position. The entrance of King John in 1497 interrupted his rule, which he recovered in 1501. His name should not be confused with Sten Sture the Younger.
people.JUAN2NORD: Son of Christian I and Dorothy. He ruled Denmark and Norway before taking the Swedish crown in 1497.
people.CRISTINASAJDIN: Wife of King John and daughter of the House of Wettin. She defended Stockholm during the Swedish rebellion of 1501 and was imprisoned after the capitulation. She was the mother of Christian II: her experience illustrates the fragility of the common government before the last attempt to preserve the union.
people.SVANTENILSSON: Swedish regent after Sten Sture the Elder. His rule continued resistance to King John's authority. He was the father of Sten Sture the Younger, who succeeded him after a new political dispute. The title of regent expresses that authority without making him a hereditary king.
people.ESTENSTUREJOVEN: Son of Svante Nilsson and regent of Sweden. He faced Christian II and the pro-union party. He died after being wounded in the campaign of 1520; his wife Christina Gyllenstierna later led the Stockholm resistance. The defeat gave way to Christian's brief Swedish royalty.
people.GUSTAV1VASA: Founder of the Vasa dynasty and builder of the modern Swedish state. He broke the Kalmar Union, promoted the Reformation and strengthened the royal authority over the nobility and the Church.
people.CATALINASAJLAU: Consort of the Ascania dynasty. Her life was connected with Saxe-Lauenburg, Sweden.
people.MARGARITALEIJON: Consort of the Leijonhufvud dynasty. Her life was connected with Sweden.
people.ERIK14SUE: Son of Gustav Vasa, king of Sweden since 1560. It began the Swedish expansion into Estonia (Reval, 1561) and the Nordic Seven Years' War against Denmark. After the Stures' murders (1567) and his marriage to Karin Månsdotter, his brothers deposed him in 1568; he died in prison in 1577.
people.CARLOS9SUE: He was the son of Gustavo Vasa and Margaret Leijonhufvud. As duke and leader of the opposition to his nephew Sigismund, he pushed for a change of power that sidelined the Polish branch of the Swedish throne. He was the father of Gustav II Adolfo and Catherine, whose offspring led to Charles X Gustav.
people.CRISTINAHOLSTEINGOTTORP: Consort of the Holstein-Gottorp dynasty. Her life was connected with Holstein, Sweden.
people.GUSTAV2ADOLFO: King of Sweden and great military reformer. Its intervention in the Thirty Years' War made Sweden one of the major powers of the Baltic.
people.MARIAELEONORABRAND: Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Her life was connected with Brandenburg, Sweden.
people.CRISTINASUE: Queen of Sweden, daughter of Gustav II Adolf, famous for her intellectual and cultural interest. She abdicated in 1654, converted to Catholicism and spent much of the rest of her life in Rome.
people.CATALINASUEVASA: Daughter of Charles IX and Mary of the Palatinate. Her marriage to John Casimir of the Palatinate-Zweibrücken connected the Vasa with a branch of Wittelsbach. Her son Carlos X Gustavo succeeded Christina of Sweden: the dynastic change of name did not break the family continuity by female line.
people.JUANCASIMIROPALZWEI: Count palatine of the Wittelsbach dynasty. His life was connected with Palatinate, Sweden.
people.CARLOS10GUSTAVO: King of Sweden and commander of a stage of maximum Swedish military expansion. His campaigns in Poland and Denmark temporarily strengthened Sweden's hegemony in the Baltic.
people.EDUVIGELEONORA: Consort of the Holstein-Gottorp dynasty. Their life was connected with Holstein, Sweden.
people.CARLOS11SUE: King of Sweden who deeply reinforced the monarchical authority and reorganized the estate and army. He left his son Charles XII a militarily powerful and centralized state.
people.ULRICALEONORADIN: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark, Sweden.
people.CARLOS12SUE: King warrior of Sweden during the Great Northern War. His first victories were spectacular, but the defeat to Russia ended Swedish supremacy in the Baltic.
people.ULRICALEONORASUE: Sister of Charles XII, she was recognised as Queen of Sweden in 1719 in exchange for accepting a constitution that limited royal power. In 1720 she abdicated in favour of her husband, Frederick of Hesse-Kassel.
people.FEDERICO1SUE: Frederick of Hesse-Kassel, king of Sweden from 1720 on the abdication of his wife Ulrica Leonor. He reigned during the so-called Age of Liberty, with a royal power very limited by the parliament; from 1730 he was also landgrave of Hesse-Kassel.
people.ADOLFOFEDERICOSUE: King of Sweden since 1751, of the House of Holstein-Gottorp. He reigned during the Age of Freedom, with royal power very limited by the Riksdag.
people.LUISAULRICAPRUSIA: Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Their life was connected with Prussia, Sweden.
people.GUSTAV3SUE: King of Sweden and illustrious monarch who reinforced royal power through the coup of 1772. He was also an important cultural patron and was killed after an attack on the Stockholm opera.
people.SOFIAMAGDALENADIN: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Sweden.
people.GUSTAV4ADOLF: King of Sweden since 1792. The war against Russia of 1808-1809 cost him Finland and a coup d'état deposed him in 1809; he died in exile in 1837.
people.CARLOS13SUE: He ascended the Swedish throne after Gustav IV Adolf deposed. The adoption of Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte resolved the search for an heir. In 1814 he also became king of Norway after the war and the constitutional agreement; the new union retained its own Norwegian institutions.
people.CARLOS14JUAN: Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was marshal to Napoleon before being elected Swedish heir and adopted by Charles XIII. As Crown Prince he led the policy that led to union with Norway.
people.DESIREECLARY: Consort of the Clary dynasty. Their life was connected with Sweden, Norway, France.
people.OSCAR1SUE: Son of Charles XIV John, Marshal Bernadotte, King of Sweden and Norway since 1844. It pushed for moderate liberal reforms, such as hereditary equality between sons and daughters.
people.MARIAPALATINADOSUE: Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Her life was connected with Palatinate, Sweden.
people.SOFIADINVALDEMAR: Consort of the Estridsen dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Sweden.
people.DOROTHEABRAND: She married first Christopher of Bavaria and, after being widowed, Christian I. This marriage continuity connected two different succession solutions for Denmark. She was the mother of John and Frederick I and defended her own heritage interests; her role does not come down to being a link between two kings.
people.ELISADENBRAND: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Brandenburg.
people.LOUISEGBDEN: Consort of the Hannover dynasty. Their life was connected with England, Denmark.
people.CAROLINEMATILDA: Consort of the Hannover dynasty. Their life was connected with England, Denmark.
people.FRED1DEN: Younger son of Christian I and uncle of Christian II. He was elected king after his nephew was deposed in 1523, while Gustav Vasa consolidated the Swedish break.
people.ANNABRANDDEN: Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Her life was connected with Brandenburg, Denmark.
people.SOPHIEPOMDEN: Consort of the Grifo dynasty. Her life was connected with Pomerania, Denmark, Holstein.
people.CHRISTIAN3DEN: Son of Frederick I. His victory in the Count's War consolidated the monarchy and made it possible to implement the Lutheran Reformation. The reorganization of Norway reinforced its subordination to the Danish crown. The continuity of the common monarch thus coincided with a profound change in institutions.
people.DOROTHEALAUDEN: Consort of the Ascania dynasty. Their life was connected with Saxe-Lauenburg, Denmark.
people.FRED2DEN: King of Denmark and Norway between 1559 and 1588. He fought Sweden in the Norse Seven Years' War, collected the Sund toll and protected astronomer Tycho Brahe.
people.SOPHIEMECKDEN: Consort of the Mecklemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Norway.
people.CHRISTIAN4DEN: King of Denmark and Norway for almost six decades. He pursued an active economic and naval policy, but his intervention in the Thirty Years' War ended up weakening the Danish position.
people.ANNECATHBRANDDEN: Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Her life was connected with Brandenburg, Denmark.
people.FRED3DEN: King of Denmark and Norway since 1648. After the defeats of Sweden, in which Escania lost, he imposed in 1660 the hereditary and absolute monarchy, fixed in the Regia Law of 1665.
people.SOPHIEAMALIEBRUN: Consort of the Welf dynasty. Her life was connected with Brunswick, Denmark.
people.CHRISTIAN5DEN: King of Denmark and Norway between 1670 and 1699. He consolidated the absolute monarchy with a new service nobility and the Danish and Norwegian legal codes of 1683 and 1687.
people.CHARLOTTEAMALIEHESSE: Consort of the Hesse dynasty. Her life was connected with Hesse, Denmark.
people.FRED4DEN: King of Denmark and Norway from 1699 to 1730. He participated in the Great Northern War against Sweden and obtained the Gottorpian part of Schleswig in 1720.
people.LOUISEMECKDEN: Consort of the Mecklemburgo dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark.
people.CHRISTIAN6DEN: King of Denmark and Norway between 1730 and 1746, of strong pietist devotion. His reign was peaceful and marked by the construction of Christiansborg Palace.
people.SOPHIEMAGDKULM: Consort of the Hohenzollern dynasty. Her life was connected with Brandenburg, Denmark.
people.FRED5DEN: King of Denmark and Norway between 1746 and 1766. His reign, largely ruled by ministers such as Bernstorff and Moltke, remained neutral and favored trade and the arts.
people.CHRISTIAN7DEN: King of Denmark and Norway since 1766, suffering from a serious mental illness. Struensee until 1772 and from 1784 his son, the future Frederick VI.
people.FRED6DEN: He held the regency for years before succeeding Christian VII. The Napoleonic Wars ended with the loss of Norway in 1814. The transfer agreed at Kiel did not produce a peaceful and immediate transfer to Sweden: there was a Norwegian constitutional movement, a war and a new agreement.
people.AUGUSTADENHG: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark, Holstein.
people.FREDERICAAMALIADEN: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark, Holstein.
people.HEDVIGSOPHIASUE: Consort of the Wittelsbach dynasty. Their life was connected with Sweden, Holstein.
people.MARGARETSCOTNOR: Princess of the Dunkeld dynasty. Her life was connected with Scotland, Norway.
people.ERIK2NORWAY: Son of Magnus VI and Ingeborg of Denmark. His marriage to Margaret of Scotland made him the father of the so-called Virgin of Norway, a Scottish heiress who died before settling in the kingdom. When Erik died without a surviving son, his brother Haakon V succeeded him.
people.MAIDNORWAY: Granddaughter of Alexander III and recognised heir to the Scottish crown. She died in 1290 during the voyage to Scotland, sparking the succession dispute known as the Great Cause.
people.MARGDINESCOCIA: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Her life was connected with Denmark, Norway, Scotland.
people.DOROTHEADENBRUN: Consort of the Oldemburgo dynasty. Their life was connected with Denmark, Brunswick.
people.HAAKON4NOR: His reign closed the long stage of Norwegian civil wars and strengthened the monarchy. Expansion to Iceland and Greenland broadened its Atlantic horizon. His son Magnus VI continued the dynasty; along that line descend Haakon V, Ingeborg of Norway and the kings who united Norway and Sweden.
people.MARGRETESKULE: Margarita, daughter of Duke Skule Bårdsson, married Haakon IV. The alliance did not prevent the subsequent confrontation between her father and her husband. She was the mother of Magnus VI: her descendants link medieval Norwegian consolidation with the Scandinavian unions of the 14th century.
people.MAGNUS6NOR: Known as the Legislator for compiling a common law for Norway. His marriage to Ingeborg of Denmark connected the neighboring royal houses. Their sons Erik II and Haakon V reigned successively; their daughters both carried the succession to Scotland and Sweden.
people.ERIK4DEN: Danish king of the House of Estridsen, died during the conflict with his brother Abel. His daughter Ingeborg's marriage to Magnus VI linked his offspring to Norway. That connection allows the legacy to be traced back to Haakon V and his grandson Magnus Eriksson.
people.INGEBORGERIKNOR: Daughter of Erik IV of Denmark and wife of Magnus VI of Norway. She was the mother of the kings Erik II and Haakon V. After Magnus' death she participated in the government during Erik's minority, in a context of tensions between the crown, aristocracy and the Church.
people.HAAKON5NOR: He succeeded his brother Erik II. Her daughter Ingeborg married Swedish prince Erik Magnusson; their son Magnus inherited Norway in 1319. That female-line transmission allowed the Norwegian crown to coincide with the Swedish choice of the same child.
people.EUFEMIARUGENNOR: Wife of Haakon V and mother of Ingeborg of Norway. Her court is associated with the dissemination of Swedish-translated knightly romances, the so-called Eufemiavisor.
people.OLAF2NORD: Son of Margaret and Haakon VI. He was elected king of Denmark as a child and inherited Norway upon the death of his father. His mother ran the government. Olaf's death without issue in 1387 forced him to seek another successive solution and paved the way for the recognition of Margaret and Eric of Pomerania.
people.INGEBORGVALDEMAR: Daughter of Valdemar IV and sister of Margaret. Her marriage to Henry of Mecklemburg linked the Danish house with a family that also claimed rights in Sweden. Through her daughter Maria was the grandmother of Eric of Pomerania: this is the family connection that made her promotion by Margarita possible.
people.PHILIPPAENGLAND: Daughter of Henry IV of England and Mary of Bohun. Her marriage to Eric of Pomerania connected the monarchy of Lancaster with Kalmar.
people.ERIKJOHVASA: Swedish nobleman and father of Gustav Vasa. He was executed in the Stockholm bloodbath of 1520. His death belongs to the context of his son's rebellion against Christian II; Gustav's accession to the throne was the result of that struggle and an election, not the inheritance of a paternal crown.
people.CECILIAMANSDOTTER: Member of the Eka family and mother of Gustavo Vasa. After the fall of Stockholm she was taken captive to Denmark, where she died. Its history shows the family consequences of the Kalmar crisis and connects Gustav's noble origin with the political breakdown of Sweden.
people.INGEBORGTOTTSTURE: Wife of Svante Nilsson and mother of Sten Sture the Younger. Her maternal lineage helps distinguish the two generations of Swedish regents. Sharing the name Sture does not make them all a direct succession from father to son; the tree preserves here the documented relationship between Svante and Sten.
people.CHRISTINAGYLLEN: Wife of Sten Sture the Younger. After her husband's death in 1520 she led the Stockholm resistance against Christian II and negotiated its capitulation. She was imprisoned after the conquest. Her son Svante extended the presence of the Stures in the nobility of Vasa Sweden.
people.SVANTESTURE: The son of Sten Sture the Younger and Christina Gyllenstierna. He developed his career under the Vasa monarchy and received the rank of count. He was one of the victims of the Sture massacres ordered by Erik XIV in 1567, an episode that exacerbated the reign's crisis.
people.ENGELBREKT: Noble miner who led the Swedish revolt against Erich of Pomerania in 1434. Elected captain of the kingdom in 1435, he was assassinated in 1436.
people.KNUD6DEN: King of Denmark since 1182, son of Valdemar I. He refused to surrender vassalry to the emperor and extended Danish rule over the southern Baltic.
people.VALDEMAR2DEN: King of Denmark since 1202. He conquered Estonia in 1219; after his defeat at Bornhöved (1227) he lost almost all his possessions in northern Germany. He passed the Jutland law.
people.ABELDEN: King of Denmark since 1250, suspected of ordering the death of his brother Erik IV. He died in 1252 in a campaign against the Frisians.
people.CHRIST1DEN: King of Denmark since 1252, brother of Erik IV and Abel. His reign was marked by a confrontation with the Archbishop of Lund.
people.ERIK5DEN: Erik Klipping, King of Denmark since 1259. He had to accept a letter in 1282 limiting royal power and was assassinated in 1286.
people.ERIK6DEN: Erik Menved, King of Denmark since 1286. He sought to dominate northern Germany and the Baltic, but his wars left the crown in debt and in debt.
people.CHRIST2DEN: King of Denmark in 1320–1326 and 13291332. His weakness against the German nobility and creditors led to the collapse of almost the entire kingdom, which was without a king until 1340.
people.VALDEMAR3DEN: Duke of Schleswig, was installed as king of Denmark between 1326 and 1329 by his uncle, Count Gerard III of Holstein, during the expulsion of Christopher II. He renounced the crown and retained Schleswig.

notes: The map distinguishes formal sovereignty from effective territorial administration: it does not include Urbino, Ferrara or the Roman lordships before their effective incorporation. Regional courts are annual approximations, not boundaries of each vicariate.

persona.resumen: One of the most powerful popes of the Middle Ages. He was active in European politics, convened the IV Lateran Council and exercised strong tutelage over kings and crusaders.

Cencio Savelli, a Camarlian of the Church and tutor of the young Frederick II, was pope between 1216 and 1227. He approved the Dominican order (1216) and Franciscan rule (1223), and crowned Emperor Frederick II in 1220.
Pope with strong legal and political personality, great adversary of Frederick II. His pontificate reinforced the papal Inquisition and deepened the conflict between the papacy and the Empire.
Goffredo da Castiglione was elected in 1241 in a conclave closed by Senator Matteo Rosso Orsini and died seventeen days later. After his death, the seat was vacant for almost two years.
Pope confronted Frederick II in the final phase of the great conflict between papacy and Empire. The Council of Lyon of 1245 declared the emperor deposed and radicalised the political struggle.

Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni, nephew of Gregory IX, was pope between 1254 and 1261. He continued the struggle against the Hohenstaufen in the kingdom of Sicily and canonized St. Clare of Assisi in 1255.

Jacques Pantaléon, son of a Troyes shoemaker and former Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, was pope between 1261 and 1264. He instituted the feast of Corpus Christi and offered the kingdom of Sicily to Charles of Anjou in front of Manfredo.

Guy Foulques, a Provencal jurist and adviser to Louis IX, became a clergyman when he was widowed and was pope between 1265 and 1268. He invested the kingdom of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, who defeated Manfredo at Benevento (1266) and Conradino at Tagliacozzo (1268).
Pope elected after a very long vacancy. He pushed in the Council of Lyon of 1274 new rules for the pontifical election, origin of the conclave system.
Pierre de Tarentaise, Dominican theologian and archbishop of Lyon, was the first pope of the order of preachers. He ruled the Church for only a few months in 1276.
Ottobuono Fieschi, nephew of Innocent IV and legate in England during the Barons' War, was elected in 1276 and died a little over a month later, having not received priestly ordination.

Portuguese physician and philosopher, traditionally identified with Pedro Hispano, author of the Summulae logicales, was pope from 1276. He died in 1277 when the roof of his stay in Viterbo's palace collapsed.

Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, of the great Roman family, was pope between 1277 and 1280. He obtained from Rudolf of Habsburg the renunciation of the Roman Empire and favored his relatives, so Dante places him among the Simonics.

Simon de Brion, French and former chancellor of Louis IX, was pope between 1281 and 1285. He supported Charles of Anjou after the Sicilian Vespers (1282), excommunicated Peter III of Aragon and offered his kingdom to Charles of Valois, son of the king of France.
Giacomo Savelli, nephew of Honorius III, was pope between 1285 and 1287. He continued to support the Angevinists against the Crown of Aragon in the war for Sicily.
Girolamo Masci, former general of the Franciscans, was the first pope of that order (1288–1292). He pushed missions into Asia and saw Acre, the last bastion crossed in the Holy Land, fall in 1291.

Pietro da Morrone, an Abruzzo hermit, was elected pope in 1294 after more than two years of vacant office. He gave up at five months, and his successor Boniface VIII kept him in custody until his death in 1296.
Pope of strong theocratic conception, facing Philip IV of France head on. His pontificate culminated in the Anagni crisis, a symbol of the retreat of the papal political power against the monarchies.

Niccolò Boccasini, the general master of the Dominicans, was elected in 1303, after the death of Boniface VIII. He lifted some of the convictions against Philip IV of France and died in Perugia after eight months of pontificate.
French Pope whose pontificate was linked to the transfer of the pontifical court to Avignon and the suppression of the Order of the Temple under the pressure of Philip IV of France.
Pope of Avignon whose long pontificate was marked by conflicts with Louis IV of Bavaria and by a strong financial and administrative reorganization of the curia.
Jacques Fournier, Cistercian and inquisitor at Pamiers, was pope at Avignon between 1334 and 1342. He began the construction of the palace of the Popes and reformed the religious orders.

Pierre Roger, Benedictine and chancellor of Philip VI of France, was pope at Avignon between 1342 and 1352. He bought the city from Queen Joanna of Naples in 1348 and expanded the palace with a lavish court.
Étienne Aubert, a lemosine jurist, was pope at Avignon between 1352 and 1362. He sent Cardinal Gil de Albornoz to recover for the Holy See the government of the Pontifical States.
William of Grimoard, Benedictine and canonist, was pope between 1362 and 1370. He returned to Rome in 1367, but returned to Avignon in 1370 and died there that same year.
Pierre Roger de Beaufort, nephew of Clement VI, was the last pope of Avignon. He moved the court to Rome in 1377, and his death, the following year, preceded the schism of the West.
Bartholomew Prignan, archbishop of Bari, was elected in Rome in 1378. His harshness led the cardinals to elect Clement VII, and so began the schism of the West.
Pietro Tomacelli, a Neapolitan, was the pope of Roman obedience between 1389 and 1404, during the schism. He restored pontifical authority in Rome and the Church States.
Cosimo Migliorati was the pope of Roman obedience between 1404 and 1406. A revolt in Rome forced him to take refuge in Viterbo in 1405.
Angelo Correr, Venetian, was the Roman pope of the Schism between 1406 and 1415. He resigned before the Council of Constance to allow the election of Martin V and the end of the schism.
Pope whose election at the Council of Constance put an end to the Great Schism of the West. His return to Rome began the political reconstruction of the Papal States.

Gabriele Condulmer, a Venetian and nephew of Gregory XII, was pope between 1431 and 1447. He opposed the Council of Basel and presided at Florence (1439) over the ephemeral union with the Greek Church.
Humanist Pope and patron saint who promoted the cultural renewal of Rome. His library and artistic projects prepared the great papal patronage of the Renaissance.
His election as Callixtus III led for the first time the Borgians to the pontificate. It spurred resistance to the Ottoman advance after the fall of Constantinople.
Pope humanist, diplomat and writer, formerly known as Eneas Silvio Piccolomini. He defended a renewed crusade against the Ottomans and left valuable autobiographical writings.
Pietro Barbo, Venetian and nephew of Eugene IV, was pope between 1464 and 1471. He built the palace of St. Mark, today Palazzo Venezia, and dissolved the Roman academy of Pomponio Leto.
A Renaissance pope who strengthened his family's power through nepotism and promoted great works in Rome. He gave the Sistine Chapel its name and was involved in Italian politics of his time.

Giovanni Battista Cibo, a Genoese, was pope between 1484 and 1492. He published the bull against the witchcraft Summis desiderantes (1484) and married his son Franceschetto to a daughter of Lorenzo de Medici.

Pope Alexander VI, member of the Borja family and one of the most controversial figures of the Renaissance papacy. His pontificate was deeply intertwined with Italian politics and the promotion of his children.
Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini, nephew of Pius II, was elected in September 1503 and died twenty-six days later.

The Renaissance pope, political commander and great patron. He pushed the reconstruction of St. Peter's and commissioned decisive works to Michelangelo, Raphael and Bramante while fighting to strengthen the Pontifical States.
Pope Medici and the great patrons of the Renaissance. His pontificate coincided with the beginning of Luther's Reformation and with an intense Italian and cultural politics.
Hadrian of Utrecht, preceptor of Charles V and governor of Castile during the Communities, was pope between 1522 and 1523. He was the last non-Italian pope until 1978.
Pope Medici caught between Francis I and Charles V during the Italian wars. His pontificate was marked by the plunder of Rome in 1527 and by the marital crisis of Henry VIII.
Pope Farnesius who promoted Catholic renewal and called the Council of Trent. His pontificate was decisive in the institutionalization of the Counter-Reformation.
Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte, one of the presidents of the Council of Trent, was pope between 1550 and 1555. He reopened the council in 1551 and built the villa Giulia in Rome.
Marcello Cervini, humanist and president of the Council of Trent, was pope for twenty-two days in 1555. Palestrina dedicated the Mass of the Papae Marcelli to him.

Gian Pietro Carafa, co-founder of the Teatinos and reorganizer of the Roman Inquisition, was pope between 1555 and 1559. He created the ghetto of Rome, enacted the first Index of Forbidden Books and confronted Philip II.

Giovanni Angelo Medici, Milanese unrelated to the Medici of Florence, was pope between 1559 and 1565. He reopened and concluded the Council of Trent (1562~1563); his nephew Carlos Borromeo led his government.
Pope Dominic and central figure of the Catholic Reformation. He promoted the application of Trent and the Holy League which defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto in 1571.
Pope known for the reform of the calendar that bears his name. He also promoted Catholic education and the strengthening of Counter-Reformation institutions.
Pope of brief but energetic pontificate, he reorganized the administration of the curia and transformed Rome urbanistically through great works and new monumental paths.
Giovanni Battista Castagna was pope for thirteen days in 1590 and died of malaria before his coronation.
Niccolò Sfondrati, bishop of Cremona, was pope from 1590 to 1591. He supported the Catholic League against Henry of Navarre in France's wars of religion.
Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti, Bolognese, was pope for two months in 1591.
Ippolito Aldobrandini was pope between 1592 and 1605. He absolved Henry IV of France (1595), incorporated Ferrara into the Church States (1598) and presided over the jubilee of 1600.
Alessandro de' Medici, of the Florentine family, was elected in April 1605 and died twenty-seven days later.
Camillo Borghese was pope from 1605 to 1621. He launched the Endeavour against Venice (1606) and finished the facade of St. Peter; his nephew Scipione Borghese assembled a large art collection.

Alessandro Ludovisi, a Bolognese, was pope from 1621 to 1623. He created the Congregation of Propaganda Fide (1622), regulated the conclave by secret ballot and canonized Ignatius of Loyola and Francisco Javier.
Pope Barberini during the Thirty Years' War. His pontificate combined great artistic patronage, family politics and the famous trial against Galileo.
Giovanni Battista Pamphilj was pope from 1644 to 1655. He protested the peace of Westphalia and commissioned Bernini to source the Four Rivers; Velázquez painted his portrait in 1650.

Fabio Chigi, Sienese and nuncio to Münster during the negotiations of Westphalia, was pope between 1655 and 1667. He commissioned Bernini to write the column in St. Peter's Square and received Christina of Sweden in Rome.
Giulio Rospigliosi, librettist and diplomat, was pope between 1667 and 1669. He mediated the peace of Aachen (1668) and supported Venice in the defense of Candia.
Emilio Altieri was elected in 1670, at almost eighty years of age, and his adopted nephew, Cardinal Paluzzo Altieri, led the government until his death in 1676.
Pope reformer and opponent of the ecclesiastical policy of Louis XIV. He supported the European resistance to the Ottoman advance of the late 17th century.
Pietro Ottoboni, Venetian, was pope between 1689 and 1691. He helped Venice in the war against the Ottomans and condemned the Gallic Declaration of 1682.

Antonio Pignatelli, of the Cerchiara branch, was pope as Innocent XII. His parents were Francesco Pignatelli of Spinazzola and Porzia Carafa; the pontifical career should not be confused with the Neapolitan family lordships.

Giovanni Francesco Albani was pope from 1700 to 1721. In the War of Spanish Succession he had to recognize Arch Duke Charles as king of Spain (1709), and he condemned Jansenism with the Bull Unigenitus (1713).
Michelangelo Conti, of the same family as Innocent III, was pope between 1721 and 1724.
Pietro Francesco Orsini, Dominican and Archbishop of Benevento, was pope from 1724 to 1730. He left the government in the hands of his secretary, Cardinal Niccolò Coscia.
Lorenzo Corsini, Florentine, was pope between 1730 and 1740. Blind since 1732, he condemned Freemasonry in 1738 and undertook the construction of the Trevi fountain.
Prospero Lambertini, a Bolognese canonist, was pope from 1740 to 1758. He signed concordates with Spain and other states and kept correspondence with scholars of the Enlightenment.
Carlo Rezzonico, Venetian, was pope from 1758 to 1769. He defended the Society of Jesus against its expulsion from Portugal, France, Spain and Naples.
Lorenzo Ganganelli, a Franciscan convent, was pope from 1769 to 1774. Pressured by the Bourbons, he suppressed the Society of Jesus in 1773.
Pope between 1775 and 1799. He faced the ecclesiastical reforms of Joseph II and the French Revolution; French troops occupied Rome and died a prisoner in Valence.

gobiernos.nota: Roman Republic and captivity: no effective territorial control of Rome.

persona.resumen: Pope between 1775 and 1799. He faced the ecclesiastical reforms of Joseph II and the French Revolution; French troops occupied Rome and died a prisoner in Valence.

gobiernos.nota: Territorial restoration of 1800; Roman/Tuscian conservative core. Election March 14th, coronation March 21st. The occupation of 1809 demands a separate condition and is not published as effective control.

persona.resumen: Barnaba Chiaramonti, a Benedictine born in Cesena in 1742, was elected in Venice in 1800. He signed the Concordat with Napoleon (1801), attended his coronation (1804) and was his prisoner between 1809 and 1814; he died in 1823.

personas.resumen: Pope elected after a very long vacancy. He pushed in the Council of Lyon of 1274 new rules for the pontifical election, origin of the conclave system.

Pope Alexander VI, member of the Borja family and one of the most controversial figures of the Renaissance papacy. His pontificate was deeply intertwined with Italian politics and the promotion of his children.
His election as Callixtus III led for the first time the Borgians to the pontificate. It spurred resistance to the Ottoman advance after the fall of Constantinople.
Noble of the Cattanei dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Noble of the Trastámara dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
Theologian of the Aquino dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Condottiere of the Hawkwood dynasty. Their life was connected with Florence, Milan, Papal States.
Condottiere of the Barbiano dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States, Naples.
Condottiere of the Fortebraccio dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States, Naples.
Condottiere of the Narni dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Lord of Fano, 1385 to 1427. Lord of the Malatesta dynasty.
Consort of the Atti dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Lord of Rimini, 1432 to 1468. Lord of the Malatesta dynasty.
Count of Urbino, 1404–1443. Count of the Montefeltro dynasty.
Condotiero, Duke of Urbino and one of the great humanist princes of the Italian Renaissance. He combined a successful military career with a courthouse famous for its culture and patronage.
Condottiere of the Colonna dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
Condottiere of the Colonna dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
Noble of the Colonna dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
Condottiere of the Médici dynasty. Their life was connected with Florence, Papal States.
Condottiere of the Vitelli dynasty. Their life was connected with Florence, Papal States.
Condottiere of the Alviano dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
One of the most powerful popes of the Middle Ages. He was active in European politics, convened the IV Lateran Council and exercised strong tutelage over kings and crusaders.

Cencio Savelli, a Camarlian of the Church and tutor of the young Frederick II, was pope between 1216 and 1227. He approved the Dominican order (1216) and Franciscan rule (1223), and crowned Emperor Frederick II in 1220.
Pope with strong legal and political personality, great adversary of Frederick II. His pontificate reinforced the papal Inquisition and deepened the conflict between the papacy and the Empire.
Goffredo da Castiglione was elected in 1241 in a conclave closed by Senator Matteo Rosso Orsini and died seventeen days later. After his death, the seat was vacant for almost two years.
Pope confronted Frederick II in the final phase of the great conflict between papacy and Empire. The Council of Lyon of 1245 declared the emperor deposed and radicalised the political struggle.

Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni, nephew of Gregory IX, was pope between 1254 and 1261. He continued the struggle against the Hohenstaufen in the kingdom of Sicily and canonized St. Clare of Assisi in 1255.

Jacques Pantaléon, son of a Troyes shoemaker and former Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, was pope between 1261 and 1264. He instituted the feast of Corpus Christi and offered the kingdom of Sicily to Charles of Anjou in front of Manfredo.

Guy Foulques, a Provencal jurist and adviser to Louis IX, became a clergyman when he was widowed and was pope between 1265 and 1268. He invested the kingdom of Sicily to Charles of Anjou, who defeated Manfredo at Benevento (1266) and Conradino at Tagliacozzo (1268).
Pierre de Tarentaise, Dominican theologian and archbishop of Lyon, was the first pope of the order of preachers. He ruled the Church for only a few months in 1276.
Ottobuono Fieschi, nephew of Innocent IV and legate in England during the Barons' War, was elected in 1276 and died a little over a month later, having not received priestly ordination.

Portuguese physician and philosopher, traditionally identified with Pedro Hispano, author of the Summulae logicales, was pope from 1276. He died in 1277 when the roof of his stay in Viterbo's palace collapsed.

Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, of the great Roman family, was pope between 1277 and 1280. He obtained from Rudolf of Habsburg the renunciation of the Roman Empire and favored his relatives, so Dante places him among the Simonics.

Simon de Brion, French and former chancellor of Louis IX, was pope between 1281 and 1285. He supported Charles of Anjou after the Sicilian Vespers (1282), excommunicated Peter III of Aragon and offered his kingdom to Charles of Valois, son of the king of France.
Giacomo Savelli, nephew of Honorius III, was pope between 1285 and 1287. He continued to support the Angevinists against the Crown of Aragon in the war for Sicily.
Girolamo Masci, former general of the Franciscans, was the first pope of that order (1288–1292). He pushed missions into Asia and saw Acre, the last bastion crossed in the Holy Land, fall in 1291.

Pietro da Morrone, an Abruzzo hermit, was elected pope in 1294 after more than two years of vacant office. He gave up at five months, and his successor Boniface VIII kept him in custody until his death in 1296.
Pope of strong theocratic conception, facing Philip IV of France head on. His pontificate culminated in the Anagni crisis, a symbol of the retreat of the papal political power against the monarchies.

Niccolò Boccasini, the general master of the Dominicans, was elected in 1303, after the death of Boniface VIII. He lifted some of the convictions against Philip IV of France and died in Perugia after eight months of pontificate.
French Pope whose pontificate was linked to the transfer of the pontifical court to Avignon and the suppression of the Order of the Temple under the pressure of Philip IV of France.
Pope of Avignon whose long pontificate was marked by conflicts with Louis IV of Bavaria and by a strong financial and administrative reorganization of the curia.
Jacques Fournier, Cistercian and inquisitor at Pamiers, was pope at Avignon between 1334 and 1342. He began the construction of the palace of the Popes and reformed the religious orders.

Pierre Roger, Benedictine and chancellor of Philip VI of France, was pope at Avignon between 1342 and 1352. He bought the city from Queen Joanna of Naples in 1348 and expanded the palace with a lavish court.
Étienne Aubert, a lemosine jurist, was pope at Avignon between 1352 and 1362. He sent Cardinal Gil de Albornoz to recover for the Holy See the government of the Pontifical States.
William of Grimoard, Benedictine and canonist, was pope between 1362 and 1370. He returned to Rome in 1367, but returned to Avignon in 1370 and died there that same year.
Pierre Roger de Beaufort, nephew of Clement VI, was the last pope of Avignon. He moved the court to Rome in 1377, and his death, the following year, preceded the schism of the West.
Bartholomew Prignan, archbishop of Bari, was elected in Rome in 1378. His harshness led the cardinals to elect Clement VII, and so began the schism of the West.
Pietro Tomacelli, a Neapolitan, was the pope of Roman obedience between 1389 and 1404, during the schism. He restored pontifical authority in Rome and the Church States.
Cosimo Migliorati was the pope of Roman obedience between 1404 and 1406. A revolt in Rome forced him to take refuge in Viterbo in 1405.

Cardinal theatrical and archbishop of Naples. He was related to Innocent XII by a branch other than the Pignatelli, not a direct nephew of the pope.

Iñigo López de Loyola, born into a family of the small Basque nobility, changed his life after being wounded in the defense of Pamplona in 1521. His spiritual experience gave rise to the Exercises. In Paris he gathered the companions of the future Society of Jesus, approved by Paul III in 1540, of which he was first superior general.
Cardinal. His career is linked to the Pontifical States.
Theologian. His career is linked to Spain, the Pontifical States.
Theologian. His career is linked to Spain, the Pontifical States.
Cardinal. His career is linked to Milan, the Pontifical States.
Cardinal of the Orsini dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Cardinal of the Colonna dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Cardinal of the Riario dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Lord of the Della Rovere dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Consort of the Montefeltro dynasty. Her life was connected with Papal States.
Duke of Urbino, 1508 to 1516. Duke of Urbino of the Della Rovere dynasty.
Cardinal of the Aldobrandini dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
Cardinal of the Borghese dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.

Nephew of Urban VIII and brother of Taddeus and Anthony, Francesco Barberini was created cardinal in 1623. He performed diplomatic and governmental functions and assembled an important library of manuscripts. After the election of Innocent X, he took refuge in France in 1646; he later returned to Rome, where he died in 1679.

The son of Carlo Barberini and Costanza Magalotti, he was one of the nephews of Urban VIII: his appointment, reserved since 1627, was made public in 1628. He shared with his brothers Francesco and Taddeo the power and patronage of the family and, after 1644, the difficulties with Innocent X. He's different from his uncle, the Capuchin cardinal of the same name.
Cardinal of the Chigi dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.

Nephew of Cardinal Mazarino, prominent figure at the court of Louis XIV and wife of Eugenio Mauricio de Savoy, Count of Soissons. Involved in the "affair of poisons", she fled France in 1680 and lived in the Spanish Netherlands; she was the mother of Prince Eugene.
Cardinal of the Médici dynasty. Their life was connected with Florence, Papal States.
Duke of the Colonna dynasty. His life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
Noble of the Trastámara-Nápoles dynasty. Her life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
Roman nobleman and admiral in the service of the Spanish Monarchy and the papacy. He commanded one of the great wings of the Holy League fleet at the Battle of Lepanto.

Barnaba Chiaramonti, a Benedictine born in Cesena in 1742, was elected in Venice in 1800. He signed the Concordat with Napoleon (1801), attended his coronation (1804) and was his prisoner between 1809 and 1814; he died in 1823.

Italian-born diplomat, cardinal and chief minister during the reign of Anna of Austria and the youth of Louis XIV. He overcame the Fronde and intervened in the negotiations of Westphalia and the peace of the Pyrenees.

eventos.titulo: The symbolic start of the Lutheran Reformation
eventos.descripcion: The controversy over indulgences makes Martin Luther the center of a dispute that soon overwhelms academic debate and questions authority, doctrine, and obedience.

The Holy League fleet, led by Don John of Austria and composed mainly of forces of the Spanish Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States, defeated the Ottoman navy of Ali Baja after hours of galley-to-galley combat. The Ottoman center collapses, Uluç Ali manages to save part of his wing and thousands of fighters are killed, wounded or captured. The victory did not drive the Ottoman Empire out of the Mediterranean, but destroyed much of its combat fleet and became a huge political and symbolic victory for the coalition.

eventos.titulo: The White Company enters Italian politics
eventos.descripcion: Companies of veterans of the Hundred Years' War, including the one associated with John Hawkwood, make the mercenary condotta a decisive force in Italian politics.

eventos.titulo: Alberico da Barbiano and the Company of San Jorge
eventos.descripcion: Alberico da Barbiano symbolizes the consolidation of arms companies led by Italian captains, capable of competing with large foreign companies.

eventos.titulo: The fall of Braccio da Montone
eventos.descripcion: The Battle of L'Aquila destroys the power of Braccio da Montone and accelerates the rise of a new generation of captains, including Francesco Sforza and Niccolò Piccinino.

Cesare Borgia eliminated several captains who had rebelled against him in Senigallia. The episode, observed by Machiavelli, summarizes the conflict between the territorial prince and the autonomous condotiers.
The Venetian defeat of Agnadello shows the Condottieri within wars already dominated by large international coalitions and armies of much larger scale.

eventos.titulo: Giovanni dalle Bande Nere is dead
eventos.descripcion: The death of Giovanni de' Medici after being wounded by artillery became a late symbol of the world of great fortune captains facing a war increasingly transformed by firearms.

eventos.titulo: Leonardo in the Rome of the Medici
eventos.descripcion: Leonardo settled in Rome under the protection of Giuliano de' Medici during the pontificate of Leo X.

eventos.titulo: Paul III approves the Society of Jesus
eventos.descripcion: The approval of the Society of Jesus gives institutional form to one of the most dynamic forces of Catholic renewal, active in education, mission and theological controversy.
The council clarified Catholic doctrine and approved disciplinary reforms in three major phases, under three pontificates, while the confessional division of Europe became permanent.
The final phase of the Council culminates in a program of doctrinal definition and ecclesiastical reform that will shape modern Catholicism.

eventos.titulo: Nicholas III and the Ascension of the Orsini
eventos.descripcion: The election of Giovanni Gaetano Orsini as Nicholas III places one of the great Roman baronial families at the center of the pontifical government and favors a wide network of relatives and clients.
The conflict between Boniface VIII and the Colonna transforms a rivalry of Roman families into a political and ecclesiastical crisis of European scope.

eventos.titulo: Martin V and the Colonna's Return
eventos.descripcion: The Council of Constance elects Oddone Colonna as Martin V, closing the Western Schism and returning to Rome a recognized pontifical head.

eventos.titulo: Sixtus IV and the Della Rovere–Riario network
eventos.descripcion: Sixtus IV makes Della Rovere and Riario's nephews cardinals, rulers and pieces of a new family policy within the Pontifical States.
Rodrigo Borja ascends to the pontificate as Alexander VI and the career of his sons makes the Borgia family an Italian political power.

eventos.titulo: Julius II and the restoration of Della Rovere
eventos.descripcion: Giuliano della Rovere becomes Julius II and combines the territorial recovery of the papacy with a family network linked to Senigallia and Urbino.

eventos.titulo: The Medici come to the papacy
eventos.descripcion: Leo X takes the Medici house to the pontifical throne; a decade later his cousin Giulio de' Medici will be Clement VII.

eventos.titulo: Paul III and the building of a Farnese dynasty
eventos.descripcion: The pontificate of Paul III combines Catholic reform with a dynastic policy that prepares the territorial ascent of his descendants in Parma and Piacenza.

eventos.titulo: Paul V and the rise of the Borghese
eventos.descripcion: The election of Camillo Borghese as Paul V makes Cardinal-nephew Scipione one of the great political, heritage and artistic beneficiaries of Baroque Rome.
Urban VIII elevated his nephews Francesco and Antonio to the cardinalate and Taddeo to the secular headship of the family, linked further to the Colonna.

eventos.titulo: Innocent X, the Pamphilj and Donna Olympia
eventos.descripcion: The pontificate of Innocent X places Olimpia Maidalchini in the center of the court and links the patrimony of Pamphilj with the Aldobrandini heritage.
Fabio Chigi becomes Alexander VII and calls Rome to his family; his nephew Flavius occupies the traditional place of the cardinal-nephew.

eventos.titulo: Innocent XI: a pope against the nepotist model
eventos.descripcion: Innocent XI avoided granting his nephew Livius the cardinalate and consciously limited the family privileges that had marked so many previous pontificates.
Innocent XII promulgated the Romanum decet Pontificem constitution, which formally restricted papal nepotism and closed a long stage of family rule of the Roman court.

eventos.titulo: Benefit: The Anjou take the kingdom
eventos.descripcion: Charles of Anjou, supported by the papacy, defeats and kills Manfredo at Benevento. The Hohenstaufen monarchy loses effective control of Sicily and Naples.

eventos.titulo: Pius V gets the Holy League
eventos.descripcion: Pius V achieves an agreement between the Spanish Monarchy, Venice and the Pontifical States. Philip II contributes an essential part of the resources and his half-brother Don John of Austria receives the supreme command of the Allied fleet.

In Messina a heterogeneous army of Spanish, Venetians, pontiffs, Genoese and other Italian contingents is concentrated. Coordinating different interests is almost as important as bringing ships together.

Pius V accompanies the coalition with public rallies, blesses the company and sends don Juan a pontifical banner. Catholic memory will then associate victory with prayers and the Rosary; the tradition that the pope knew the triumph before receiving the news belongs to the devotional tradition, not to a fact demonstrable by itself.

The League has Barbarigo in the left wing, Don Juan and Colonna in the centre, Gianandrea Doria in the right and Álvaro de Bazán in the front of the reserve. In front of them, Ali Baja leads the Ottoman center and Uluç Ali leads the wing facing Doria.

In the center, the Royal gallery of don Juan and the Sultanate of Ali Bajá are stuck in a struggle of successive approaches, archbuildings and reinforcements. The fall of Ali Baja and the capture of his ship disorganize the Ottoman center and turn the central battle into the symbolic core of victory.

eventos.titulo: Leopold and Sobieski agree to help each other
eventos.descripcion: With papal mediation, Leopold I and John III Sobieski agree a defensive alliance. If Vienna or Krakow are attacked, the other sovereign must come to the aid of the ally.

eventos.titulo: From saving Vienna to moving on to the offensive
eventos.descripcion: After the victory, a new Holy League is formed. The Habsburgs, Poland and Venice transform an emergency defense into a prolonged war against the Ottoman Empire.

people.GREG10: Pope elected after a very long vacancy. He pushed in the Council of Lyon of 1274 new rules for the pontifical election, origin of the conclave system.
people.RODRIGOBORJA: Pope Alexander VI, member of the Borja family and one of the most controversial figures of the Renaissance papacy. His pontificate was deeply intertwined with Italian politics and the promotion of his children.
people.ALFONSOBORJA: His election as Callixtus III led for the first time the Borgians to the pontificate. It spurred resistance to the Ottoman advance after the fall of Constantinople.
people.VANNOZZACATT: Noble of the Cattanei dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
people.SANCHAARAG: Noble of the Trastámara dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
people.SANTOTOMAS: Theologian of the Aquino dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
people.HAWKWOOD: Condottiere of the Hawkwood dynasty. Their life was connected with Florence, Milan, Papal States.
people.ALBERICOBARB: Condottiere of the Barbiano dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States, Naples.
people.BRACCIOMONT: Condottiere of the Fortebraccio dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States, Naples.
people.GATTAMELATA: Condottiere of the Narni dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
people.PAND3MAL: Lord of Fano, 1385 to 1427. Lord of the Malatesta dynasty.
people.ISOTTAATTI: Consort of the Atti dynasty. Their life was connected with Papal States.
people.SIGISMALAT: Lord of Rimini, 1432 to 1468. Lord of the Malatesta dynasty.
people.GUIDANTMONTE: Count of Urbino, 1404–1443. Count of the Montefeltro dynasty.
people.FEDMONTE: Condotiero, Duke of Urbino and one of the great humanist princes of the Italian Renaissance. He combined a successful military career with a courthouse famous for its culture and patronage.
people.PROSPCOLONNA: Condottiere of the Colonna dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
people.FABRCOLONNA: Condottiere of the Colonna dynasty. Their life was connected with Naples, Papal States.
